ol96b1-c16729.summary: Auriol's question whether theology's subject is God under the formality of deity, prompted by Lombard's division of his work. Opening arguments propose the whole Christ, the believable or revealable, things and signs, divine being, no subject at all, God as glorifier, God as good or end, and God as unknown; the contrary (Scotus) argues for God as deity. Article 1 rejects Scotus's definition of a subject as what first virtually contains all a science's truths: one science covers genus and species without one virtual container, it would make effects the subject of quia sciences, and it would multiply geometries endlessly. Article 2, explicitly following Aristotle and Averroes, defines a subject as a genus fixing one mode of abstraction, and classifies twelve human sciences by the intellect's reflexive, extended or purely abstract stances. Article 3 rejects Bonaventure's threefold subject, Thomas's revealable, divine being, Giles's glorifier, Thomas of Strasbourg's good, Heilmann's unknown, and Scotus's 'infinite being' as the wayfarer's subject. Article 4 concludes: the subjective character mediates all per se predication; deity is theology's subjective character and accounts for its declarative mode; the wayfarer reaches deity through a proper, analogical, proportional concept; and theology is broader than metaphysics yet not exhaustive. Theology's six-part division maps onto the four books. An appended fifth article makes bodily substance the subject of physics (motion is an attribute) and speech expressive of concepts the subject of logic. The replies affirm theology's regulative primacy over philosophy.
claims: God under the formality of deity is theology's subject.
A science's subject is a genus fixing one mode of abstraction, and its subjective character mediates all per se predication.
Virtual containment is not the defining mark of a science's subject.
The wayfarer has a proper but analogical concept of deity, prior to 'infinite being'.
Theology is declarative because deity is not naturally knowable distinctly.
Theology's six considerations correspond to the structure of the Sentences.
The subject of natural philosophy is bodily substance; that of logic is speech expressive of concepts.
Theology is broader than metaphysics and regulates philosophy.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e107.summary: Title of the question: whether the theological habit has God under the formality of deity as its subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e114.summary: Ties the question to Lombard's division of the book into titles and chapters: sciences are divided as their subjects are (De anima III), so one must ask whether theology's subject is God under the formality of deity.
claims: Sciences are divided according to their subjects.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e133.summary: Rubric for arguments that the whole Christ is theology's subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e138.summary: Argues that theology's subject is the whole Christ, not God. Augustine (Contra Faustum) says everything Moses wrote concerns Christ, by prefiguring him or commending his grace, and likewise the Prophets, while the Gospels and Epistles are chiefly about him. So Christ is the subject of all Scripture. Also, theology's subject is that of the articles, which concern Christ's divinity and humanity, so it is the whole Christ as one God and man.
claims: (Argument) All Scripture concerns Christ.
(Argument) The articles of faith concern the whole Christ.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e184.summary: Argues that a science's subject is that to which all it treats is reduced, and theology's matters (Trinity, creation and governance, redemption through Christ's passion, virtues, precepts, sacraments) reduce to the whole Christ, not to God as God, who did not suffer. (Part of the text is corrupt.)
claims: (Argument) Theology's matters are unified only in the whole Christ.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e219.summary: Rubric for arguments that the believable or revealable is the subject, citing Thomas (ST I q. 1 a. 3) and Capreolus.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e237.summary: Argues that a science that declares believed things has them as its subject, and theology does, so the believable is its subject.
claims: (Argument) Theology declares believed things, so they are its subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e253.summary: Argues that the subject is the character under which a science reaches everything it considers. Theology reaches the histories of kings, the deeds of the patriarchs, the prophets' sayings and many philosophical matters insofar as divinely revealed, so the revealable is its subject.
claims: (Argument) Theology considers everything insofar as divinely revealed.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e274.summary: Rubric for arguments that things and signs are the subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e279.summary: Argues from Augustine that all doctrine, sacred doctrine included, is of things or signs, so things and signs are theology's subject.
claims: (Argument) All sacred doctrine concerns things or signs.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e295.summary: Argues that a science is divided according to its subject, and Augustine and Lombard divide all theology by things and signs, so these are its subject.
claims: (Argument) Theology is divided by things and signs.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e311.summary: Rubric for arguments that 'divine being' is the subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e316.summary: Argues that a science's subject is predicated in common of everything determined in it, and everything treated in theology is 'divine being', so that is its subject.
claims: (Argument) A subject is predicable of all treated in the science.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e336.summary: Argues that theology's subject must be as wide as being, metaphysics' subject, or theology would be particular and subalternate to metaphysics. Only 'divine being', predicated of God and of everything from God, is that wide.
claims: (Argument) Theology's subject must be as wide as being.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e361.summary: Argues that nothing is common to what falls under Scripture's four senses (moral, literal, anagogical, allegorical) except divine being, so it is the subject.
claims: (Argument) Only divine being is common to all four senses of Scripture.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e374.summary: Rubric for arguments that God is in no way the subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e379.summary: Argues that a science's subject must have parts, attributes and principles (Posterior Analytics I), but God has no attributes (no accidents), no parts (most simple) and no principles (simply first), so he cannot be theology's subject.
claims: (Argument) A subject must have parts, attributes and principles, which God lacks.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e408.summary: Argues that a science is divided as its subject is, but theology's books are not divided according to divisions of God, who is indivisible.
claims: (Argument) God's indivisibility cannot ground theology's divisions.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e419.summary: Argues that a subject must admit several concepts (of definition and of attributes), but God, like any separate intelligence, is either known whole or not at all (Aristotle), so he cannot be a subject.
claims: (Argument) God cannot be grasped by several concepts.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e441.summary: Argues that metaphysics' subject is not theology's, and Averroes implies God is metaphysics' subject, since no science proves its subject's existence and the metaphysician does not prove God's.
claims: (Argument) God is the subject of metaphysics (Averroes).

ol96b1-c16729-d1e460.summary: Rubric for arguments that God is the subject not as deity but as glorifier.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e467.summary: Argues that a finite science cannot have an infinite character as subject, since a habit is specified by and proportioned to its object. Deity is infinite (Damascene's 'ocean of infinite substance') and our theology finite, so its subject is God under a special character, as glorifier. Confirmed: our finite science and God's infinite science cannot share the same subject under the same character.
claims: (Argument) A finite habit requires a finite formal object.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e506.summary: Argues that the formal character of the subject measures everything treated, and theology treats only truths about God ordered to our restoration and glorification (Hugh of St Victor: the works of restoration are theology's matter). So God as glorifier is its subject.
claims: (Argument) Theology treats only truths ordered to our restoration.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e530.summary: Rubric for arguments that the subject is God as good, lovable and end, citing Thomas of Strasbourg.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e539.summary: Argues that God is theology's subject under the noblest character, which is good and end: deity is good only by goodness, and without goodness what remains is not formally good. Confirmed: Avicenna says the science of the end is noblest.
claims: (Argument) Goodness and finality are God's noblest characters.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e572.summary: Argues that a practical science's object must be under the character of good, appetible and end, since it aims to have and act on its object, and theology is practical. Confirmed: speculative science concerns speculable truth, practical science operable good.
claims: (Argument) A practical science's object is the good as end.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e599.summary: Rubric for arguments that God is the subject as unknown (attributed in a marginal gloss to an opinion of Heilmann Wunnenberg, teacher of Marsilius of Inghen).

ol96b1-c16729-d1e610.summary: Argues that something is subject to a science and its principles under the same character, and God as unknown and enigmatic is the object of faith and the articles, theology's principles (faith is of the unseen; Augustine). So God is subject as unknown.
claims: (Argument) God is the object of faith as unknown.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e634.summary: Argues that God is theology's subject under the character by which it joins us to him, and it joins us to him as unknown, for we know what he is not, not what he is (Dionysius). (A rubric announcing the counter-position, that God is the subject as deity, is printed at the end.)
claims: (Argument) Theology unites us to God as unknown (negative theology).

ol96b1-c16729-d1e652.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio prologue q. 3) for the contrary.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e659.summary: Argues that God is theology's subject as deity, since the subject is the character under which it virtually contains all the science's truths, and deity, first and foundational among God's conceivable characters, contains the Trinity, omnipotence, creation and all the rest.
claims: (Argument) Deity virtually contains all truths about God.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e688.summary: Argues that the noblest habit has the noblest object under the noblest character; God is noblest of knowables and deity noblest of divine characters, the foundation of all others, so God as deity is the subject of theology, the noblest science.
claims: (Argument) Deity is the noblest divine character.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e707.summary: Argues that theology must surpass philosophy in the dignity of its subject, since it cannot in certainty (De anima I). First philosophy treats God as first cause, last end and noblest form (Metaphysics I, XII), so theology surpasses it only if its subject is God as deity.
claims: (Argument) Theology exceeds metaphysics only through the dignity of its subject.
(Argument) Metaphysics treats God as first cause and end.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e757.summary: Argues that God is theology's subject under the character by which he is the object of faith and of the blessed's vision, since these cognitions succeed one another about the same thing. The blessed see him as deity, and faith concerns him as deity, immediately in articles about the deity and mediately in those about the humanity, which concern the God-man.
claims: (Argument) Faith and beatific vision share God under the formality of deity.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e786.summary: Argues that it is better to posit God as deity as subject, since it saves everything the alternatives (Christ, divine being, things and signs, glorifier) save, equally well or better.
claims: (Argument) God as deity explains all that rival subjects explain.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e808.summary: Rubric marking the response to the question.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e813.summary: Introduces the order of the response.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e820.summary: First step: what the formal character of a science's subject or object is according to some (Scotus).

ol96b1-c16729-d1e830.summary: Second step: what it is according to Auriol.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e837.summary: Third step: survey of the doctors' opinions on the question itself.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e851.summary: Fifth step: inferences about the subject of logic, natural philosophy and other sciences.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e860.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion on what the character of a science's subject is (Ordinatio prologue q. 1 a. 2 [sic]).

ol96b1-c16729-d1e871.summary: States Scotus's definition: the character of a first object or subject is to contain virtually in itself...
claims: (Reported) The first subject virtually contains the habit's truths.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e881.summary: ...first and all truths of that habit. Scotus explains it in three ways. First, by exposition: 'first' means not depending on another while others depend on it, so to contain a habit's truths first is to contain them by one's own character, even with everything else removed, as the character of triangle contains 'has three angles'.
claims: (Reported) To contain truths 'first' is to contain them by one's own character independently of all else.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e914.summary: Continues the example: the character of triangle first contains 'has three angles', so that an isosceles would not have them without that character but would with it, everything else removed.
claims: (Reported) The isosceles has three angles through the character of triangle.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e925.summary: Scotus's second explanation, by proof: the first object virtually contains every immediate proposition, since in immediate propositions the subject contains the predicate (a proper attribute in whose definition the subject falls), and such propositions contain all conclusions. So the subject contains all the habit's truths from first to last.
claims: (Reported) The subject virtually contains all immediate propositions and thus all conclusions.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e958.summary: Scotus's further proof: the object relates to the habit as an equivocal, adequate cause, which contains its effect virtually and, if adequate, wholly. Adequacy is primacy (Posterior Analytics I's definition of the universal), so the object, as universal and adequately containing the habit, first contains it virtually.
claims: (Reported) The object is an equivocal and adequate cause of the habit.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e982.summary: Scotus's third explanation, rebutting two objections that the first object is a common predicate rather than virtually containing. First: a power's object is common to all it knows. Reply: object to power is mover to movable, where any agent of a kind can act on any patient of that kind, so common characters are the first extremes; but object to habit is cause to effect, where not every instance causes the habit, only something first virtually containing.
claims: (Reported) Object to power is mover to movable; object to habit is cause to effect.
(Reported) A power's object is common; a habit's object is a first virtual container.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1065.summary: Scotus's reply to the second objection (sciences commonly assign a common subject: line, number, being): such sciences are unified generically, not specifically. A common subject is abstracted from the objects of the specifically different habits within them.
claims: (Reported) Sciences with common subjects have only generic unity.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1086.summary: Rubric announcing, against Scotus, that virtual containment is not the character of a scientific subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1093.summary: Argues against Scotus. One science covers whole and part, genus and species (triangle and isosceles, animal and man), or there would be countless sciences. But the truths about a subject, its parts, and their attributes are not first virtually contained in any one thing: risibility belongs to man through rational, not animal, and three angles to triangle, not figure; and the whole's attributes are not contained in the parts' characters. Nor does potential containment in the genus help: virtual containment lets the intellect deduce what is contained, potential containment does not (or knowing the genus would give all species and attributes); and if species are only potentially in the genus, the genus does not contain their attributes first.
claims: One science covers a genus and its species.
No single character first virtually contains the truths about a genus and all its species.
Virtual and potential containment differ: only the former permits deduction.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1197.summary: Argues that if first virtually containing a science's truths defined the first object, whatever had it would be first object. Effects and signs virtually contain a 'quia' science's truths (its principles come from them), so they would be its first subject, which is clearly false.
claims: On Scotus's definition, effects and signs would be the subject of quia sciences, which is false.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1241.summary: Argues that on Scotus's view the subject relates to the habit as cause to effect, which holds only in propter quid science; in quia science effects cause the habit. So only propter quid would count as science with a subject, against Posterior Analytics I. And Aristotle defines a first subject as having parts, properties and attributes, which is not virtual containment, since parts and their attributes are only potentially in the genus.
claims: Quia science is genuine science and has a subject.
Aristotle's criterion for a subject is having parts and attributes, not virtual containment.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1289.summary: Argues that the object relates to the habit as cause to effect, yet one science has several partial causes: in geometry the triangle causes the part about triangles, the circle the part in Euclid III, and so on. So geometry would have several subjects, or its common subject would not virtually contain. Saying geometry is one only generically, with a specific habit per figure, fails: figures are infinite in number, so there would be infinitely many geometries; habits would multiply with every intermediate attribute and every chain of conclusions; even the subject of immediate propositions does not first contain what follows from them; and geometry has one specific mode of proceeding and one logic, so it is one species of science (previous question).
claims: A science has several partial causes among its objects.
Treating each figure as grounding a separate geometry leads to infinite sciences.
Geometry is specifically one through one mode of proceeding and one logic.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1400.summary: Turns Scotus's distinction against him. As the first extremes of the active-passive proportion are common, so are those of agent to effect: an agent of a kind can produce any effect of that kind, as any fire can kindle any fire. The object relates to the habit as agent to effect, so each species sharing the object's character partially causes the habit, and nothing specific first virtually contains the whole habit, only something common by predication. Scotus's definition holds only for a propter quid science with one indivisible specific subject and its immediate attributes, which may be what he meant.
claims: Each species under a science's object partially causes the habit.
A science's subject is common by predication, not a first virtual container.
Scotus's definition fits only a propter quid science with one specific subject.

ol96b1-c16729-Dd1e1466.summary: Auriol's own account of what makes something the subject of a science, explicitly following Aristotle and Averroes against modern innovators. A subject is a genus with parts and attributes that fixes one specific mode of knowing, namely one mode of abstraction. Aptitude by person and age shows modes of abstraction differ in kind. The twelve human sciences are mapped onto the intellect's stances: reflexive toward its own acts, modes of conceiving and the appeal of concepts (logic, grammar, rhetoric); extended to imagination (arithmetic, geometry), to sense (natural science, with medicine and moral science as particular sciences about man), or to both (harmonics, astronomy, optics); and purely abstract (metaphysics). A subject genus need not be one species or genus nor virtually contain all truths; it suffices that everything in the science reduces to it as attribute, part or principle under one uniform mode of abstraction rooted in the subject's nature.
claims: A science's subject is a genus that fixes one specific mode of abstraction.
There are twelve human sciences, distinguished by the intellect's modes of abstraction.
A subject need not virtually contain all truths; reduction suffices.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1475.summary: Heading of the second article: what makes something able to be the first subject of a science, according to Auriol.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1484.summary: Auriol declares that he will follow Aristotle and Averroes, whose philosophy was supremely examined and purged of fancies, against moderns who abandon it for novelties of their own liking. A science's subject is a subject genus with attributes and parts that fixes for itself one specific kind of cognition and one proper mode of knowing, namely one specific mode of abstraction. First proof: modes of abstraction are modes of knowing that vary with individuals (some suit mathematics, not metaphysics) and with age (a boy can be a mathematician but not a philosopher, Ethics VI, because mathematics is by abstraction and philosophy by experience).
claims: Auriol intends to follow Aristotle and Averroes against modern novelties.
A science's subject is a genus that fixes one specific mode of abstraction.
Modes of abstraction are specifically different modes of knowing, as aptitude by person and age shows.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1575.summary: Second proof: each science appropriates a mode of abstraction, and sciences are distinguished by them. There are twelve human sciences: three linguistic (grammar, logic, rhetoric, with poetics part of rhetoric), two pure mathematical (arithmetic, geometry), three sensory-experiential (natural philosophy, ethics, medicine), three intermediate (astronomy, harmonics, optics), and one purely intellectual (metaphysics). The intellect has five stances by degree of abstraction. Reflexively it turns to its own acts, and logic takes principles from experience of its simple, composing and discursive acts (valid moods, modal and categorical propositions, the ten categories); to its modes of conceiving, from which modes of signifying arise (grammar); and to the dignity and appeal of concepts (rhetoric and poetics). Extensively it reaches outward through imagination, through the external senses (especially sight and hearing), or through both.
claims: There are twelve human sciences in five groups.
Logic, grammar and rhetoric take principles reflexively from the intellect's own acts and modes.
The intellect's stances are reflexive, extended to imagination, to sense, to both, or purely abstract.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1715.summary: Continues. Extension to imagination gives the pure mathematical sciences, distinguished by degree of abstraction (greater for numbers than for situated magnitudes). Extension to pure sensibles gives natural science, which covers all sensibles, and two particular sciences under it about one special sensible, man: medicine, which preserves bodily health, and moral or civil science, under which laws and canons fall, which preserves the soul's virtue.
claims: Arithmetic is more abstract than geometry.
Medicine and moral science are particular sciences under natural science, concerned with man.
Law and canon law fall under moral science.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1761.summary: Continues. Extension to sense and imagination together gives the intermediate sciences: harmonics (imagined numerical proportions with heard experience), astronomy (imagined lines and circles with instrument-aided sight), and optics (experience of sight, including errors, with imagined lines and triangles). Purely abstract cognition gives metaphysics, the best of human sciences for its freest mode. So twelve sciences correspond to twelve specific kinds of abstraction, least in ethics and medicine, more in the intermediate sciences, more still in geometry and arithmetic, and greatest in metaphysics.
claims: Harmonics, astronomy and optics combine imagination and sense.
Metaphysics is the most abstract and best of human sciences.
Specific modes of abstraction distinguish modes of knowing.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1861.summary: Third proof and application. What makes knowables a distinct kind distinguishes modes of knowing, and knowables sharing one mode of abstraction form one kind whatever their number (one fit for one geometrical cognition is fit for all, though maybe not for metaphysics). Aristotle's 'one subject genus' is one knowable genus whose parts and attributes share one mode of abstraction and so one specific science. It need not be one species or genus: sometimes one species has its own science (number), sometimes a whole category falls with others under one. Nor need it virtually contain all truths so they can be known from its definition. It suffices that everything in the science reduces to it as attributes, parts, principles, or their attributes and principles, so that all form one uniformly abstracted knowable, the uniformity coming from the subject's nature, as arithmetical abstraction from number and natural science's concern with sensibles from bodily substance.
claims: Aristotle's 'one subject genus' is a knowable genus unified by one mode of abstraction.
A subject need not be one species or genus, nor virtually contain all truths.
It suffices that everything in a science reduces to the subject as attribute, part or principle.
The uniform mode of abstraction arises from the nature of the common subject.

ol96b1-c16729-Dd1e1964.summary: Surveys and rejects the doctors' views on theology's subject. Bonaventure's threefold subject (God as radical principle, the whole Christ as integral whole, things and signs or the believable as universal whole) is beautiful but improper: God is principally intended, not a radical principle; integral containment does not make a subject (Socrates), and Trinitarian truths do not reduce to Christ; a predicate common to everything is an attribute, and things and signs belong to theology only as divine. Thomas's revealable is a relation of reason, inadequate (revelations outside theology), and inconsistent with making God the subject. Divine being is a mere denomination considered for God's sake. Giles's God as glorifier is either deity itself or a contingent denomination, and the Trinity does not belong to God as glorifier. God as good or end (Thomas of Strasbourg) is a relation of reason. God as unknown is opposed to science. Scotus rightly makes God as deity the subject in itself, but wrongly makes 'infinite being' the wayfarer's first concept: theologians ask whether God is infinite, attribute many predicates to a prior concept 'God', and can form analogical concepts, and 'pure act' is no less intimate.
claims: God, not Christ, things and signs, the revealable, or divine being, is theology's subject.
Relations of reason and denominations cannot be a real science's formal object.
God as deity is theology's subject in itself.
The wayfarer's concept of God is prior to 'infinite being'.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1973.summary: Heading of the third article, which surveys the doctors, beginning with Bonaventure: Christ, God, and things and signs are each theology's subject in different senses (Sentences I, prologue q. 1).

ol96b1-c16729-d1e1984.summary: Begins Bonaventure's view: the whole Christ is in some way the subject, with 'subject' taken in three senses. First, that to which all reduces as to a radical principle, as letters in grammar and the point in geometry; in this sense God is theology's subject.
claims: (Reported) As radical principle, God is theology's subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2013.summary: Continues Bonaventure: second, that to which all reduces as to an integral whole, as the complete sentence in grammar or body (containing all dimensions) in geometry; in this sense Christ, comprising divine and human natures and head and members, is theology's subject. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: (Reported) As integral whole, the whole Christ is theology's subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2038.summary: Continues Bonaventure: third, that to which all reduces as to a universal whole, as articulated sound in grammar or immobile continuous quantity in geometry; in this sense things and signs, or the believable as intelligible, are theology's subject. The view rests on the first three groups of arguments. Auriol finds it beautifully said and right about God but improper on three points.
claims: (Reported) As universal whole, things and signs or the believable are theology's subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2071.summary: First two criticisms of Bonaventure. God is not theology's subject as a radical principle like the point or letter, since those are not what geometer and grammarian chiefly intend, while God is first intended by the theologian, and what is principally intended cannot be a radical principle. And integral containment is no criterion of subject: in Socrates are quiddity and accidents, act and potency, matter and form, motion, time, soul, sleep and waking, yet Socrates is the subject of neither metaphysics nor physics.
claims: God is principally intended by theology, not a radical principle.
Containing a science's matters integrally does not make something its subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2136.summary: Further criticism. 'The Holy Spirit is God' is a theological proposition that does not reduce to Christ as an integral whole, since Christ is not composed of it, nor do the persons' distinctions and emanations. Third criticism: things and signs as a universal predicable are not the subject, since what is predicated of all a science treats is an attribute, not the subject (truth in metaphysics, sensibility in physics, infinite divisibility in geometry, even and odd in arithmetic). (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: Trinitarian truths do not reduce to Christ as an integral whole.
A predicate common to all a science treats is an attribute, not the subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2199.summary: Further criticism: even if things and signs are predicated of everything theological, other sciences are about things (physics) or signs (grammar), so they belong to the theologian only as divine. God, not things and signs, is the object.
claims: Things and signs belong to theology only as divine, so God is the object.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2217.summary: Rubric naming Thomas's opinion that the divinely revealable is the subject (ST I q. 1).

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2224.summary: States the view that theology's formal object is the divinely revealable, everything it considers sharing that character, supported by the second group of arguments. Auriol replies that no real, most noble science has a relation of reason as formal object, and 'revealable' adds only a relation of reason to God to the theological truths.
claims: (Reported) The revealable is theology's formal object.
A relation of reason cannot be the formal object of a real science.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2256.summary: Further objection: the object must be adequate to the science, neither exceeding it nor exceeded. Much has been revealed that theology does not contain: the child to be born of a virgin revealed to philosophers, God appearing to Alexander in pontifical robes and promising him Asia, and perhaps other inspirations among the nations.
claims: The object of a science must be adequate to it.
Many revelations fall outside theology.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2282.summary: Further objection to Thomas: one science has one formal subject, and these thinkers also make God the subject, so their two claims conflict. The paragraph then states and refutes the view that 'divine being' is the subject (attributed to Thomas's Sentences commentary), supported by the fourth group of arguments. When a common character is considered only because a proper one is principally intended, the proper one is the subject: health in urine and diet serves animal health, so health in general is not medicine's subject. Divine being is intended because God is intended first. And a mere denomination taken from God cannot be a real science's formal object. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: Making both God and the revealable the subject is inconsistent.
A common character considered for the sake of a proper one is not the subject.
Divine being is a denomination from God and cannot be a real science's formal object.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2352.summary: Rubric naming Giles of Rome's opinion (Sentences I, prologue q. 3) that God as glorifier is the subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2361.summary: States Giles's view: God is the subject under the contracted character of glorifier, supported by the sixth group of arguments. Auriol asks what 'glorifier' means. If it is that by which God formally glorifies, that is deity and the divine essence, conceding Auriol's view. If it is a relation or denomination toward the glorified (as 'Creator' derives from creation in the creature), then a contingent, quasi-accidental denomination, a being per accidens, would be theology's subject, which is impossible.
claims: (Reported) God as glorifier is theology's subject.
Glorification is either deity itself or a contingent denomination, which cannot be a subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2409.summary: Further objection: God is not the subject under a character by which theology's truths do not belong to him, and the Trinity does not belong to God as glorifier, since he was triune before glorifying. Confirmed: attributes belong to a subject through the subject's character, not the reverse; God glorifies because triune or God, not the reverse.
claims: The Trinity does not belong to God as glorifier.
Attributes belong to a subject through its character, not vice versa.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2438.summary: Rubric naming the opinion (Thomas of Strasbourg) that God as good, lovable and end is the subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2450.summary: States the view that God as last end, highest good or most lovable is the subject, supported by the seventh group of arguments. It fails for the same reason: goodness, lovability and finality signify only relations of reason or denominations regarding God.
claims: (Reported) God as end or good is theology's subject.
Goodness, lovability and finality are relations of reason or denominations.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2474.summary: Rubric naming the opinion (Heilmann) that God as unknown is the subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2481.summary: States and attacks the view that God as unknown is the subject, supported by the eighth group of arguments, as even less possible. No science has as subject a character opposed to it, and every science aims to flee ignorance and remove unknownness from its object.
claims: (Reported) God as unknown is theology's subject.
No science takes as its formal character something opposed to science.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2503.summary: Further objection: no science destroys its subject's formal character, or it would destroy itself, yet every science aims to remove ignorance from its object, so unknownness cannot be a formal object.
claims: A science cannot aim to destroy its own formal object.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2519.summary: Further objection: every science seeks truths about its subject and attributes them to it as such, but theology does not attribute the Trinity to God as unknown.
claims: The Trinity is not attributed to God as unknown.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2530.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio prologue q. 3): God as deity is theology's subject in itself, but as infinite being in our intellect.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2544.summary: States Scotus's view. In itself, theology's subject is God as deity, for necessary truths (deity first virtually contains them) and contingent ones (the subject is what the first contingent predicate immediately belongs to, known only by intuition of the extremes, and being born, suffering and creating belong first only to God as deity). For our theology, which lacks evidence from its object, the subject is the most perfect concept we have closest to deity: infinite being. Infinity is an intrinsic degree more intimate than any attribute, and the articles reduce to it (three persons in one nature because God is infinite in nature). The five contrary arguments support it. Auriol accepts the account of theology in itself but rejects 'infinite being' as the wayfarer's first concept. In a question the predicate's concept must differ from the subject's (asking whether man is man asks nothing), and theologians ask whether God is infinite, so they have a concept of God other than infinite being.
claims: (Reported) God as deity is theology's subject in itself, for necessary and contingent truths.
(Reported) For wayfarers the subject is God as infinite being.
God as deity is rightly theology's subject in itself.
Since theologians ask whether God is infinite, their concept of God differs from 'infinite being'.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2703.summary: Further objection: when the intellect attributes several things to a substrate, its concept of the substrate differs from those of the attributes (Socrates is white, tall, father). The theologian says God is infinite being, pure act, first cause and much else, so his concept of 'God' differs from all of them. It will not do to say that in 'God is infinite' the concept of God is pure act or another appropriated general concept, since all can be predicated together in one proposition, and introspection does not find that 'God is infinite' means 'pure act is infinite'.
claims: The concept of a substrate differs from the concepts attributed to it.
The theologian's concept 'God' is prior to and distinct from 'infinite being', 'pure act' and the like.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2764.summary: Further objection: the metaphysician has no more absolute concept of God than the theologian, yet he conceives God prior to 'infinite being' when he demonstrates that God is infinite, attributing infinity to a prior subject. So the theologian has a concept prior to infinite being.
claims: Metaphysical demonstration of God's infinity presupposes a prior concept of God.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2788.summary: Further objection: from three known concepts the intellect can reach an analogical concept of an unknown fourth, as matter is known by analogy (figure : figurable :: formed : formable, Physics I). The theologian knows line, straight and infinite, so he can reach a fourth concept, something related to infinite as line to straight, a prior substrate of infinity.
claims: Analogical proportion yields concepts of unknown things.
The theologian can form an analogical concept of God prior to infinity.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2834.summary: Further objection: actuality is as intimate to a thing as infinity, or more so, since act signifies reality, especially of a subsisting form, and adding 'pure' makes it more intrinsic. So 'pure act' is as close to deity as 'infinite being' or closer. Confirmed: Aristotle first attributes pure act to God (Metaphysics XII). (The end is corrupt.)
claims: Pure act is at least as close to deity as infinite being.

ol96b1-c16729-Dd1e2861.summary: Gives Auriol's answer in four propositions, a fifth article on other sciences, and replies. (1) Within a subject genus, the subjective character is what mediates the subject's reception of all the science's per se predicates (not virtual containment) and whose removal destroys the science. (2) Deity is theology's subjective character: through it persons, perfections, possibles and contingent facts are attributed to God, and its natural unknowability makes theology only declarative. Theology divides into six considerations matching the Sentences (divine by essence; by assumption; by creation and governance; by precept; by institution; by beatific fulfillment), though Scripture is not so organized. (3) The wayfarer attributes all truths to a proper but obscure, analogical (proportional) concept of deity that underlies 'infinite being' and 'pure act', proportional rather than distinctive and so not beatific (more at d. 22). (4) Theology is broader than metaphysics but not exhaustive of knowable truth. The fifth article tests the definition: natural philosophy's subject is bodily substance, not mobile body, since motion and rest are attributes, as the structure of the natural books shows; logic's subject is speech as expressive of concepts, not second intentions, syllogism, mode of knowing or being of reason. The replies dismiss Christ, the believable, the revealable, things and signs, divine being, glorifier, good and end, and unknown as subjects; affirm theology's regulative superiority over metaphysics and physics; and explain God's quasi-parts, attributes and principle, the division of Scripture by attributions to God, and finite habits of an infinite object.
claims: The subjective character mediates the subject's reception of all per se predicates.
Deity is theology's subjective character and explains its declarative mode.
Theology divides into six considerations corresponding to the books of the Sentences.
The wayfarer has a proper, analogical concept of deity prior to 'infinite being'.
Theology is broader than metaphysics but not exhaustive.
Bodily substance is natural philosophy's subject; speech expressing concepts is logic's.
Theology regulates and judges metaphysics and physics.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2870.summary: Heading of the fourth article: Auriol's answer on what the subjective character (ratio subiectiva) is.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2877.summary: Announces that the answer comes in four propositions.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e2884.summary: First proposition: within the subject (a knowable genus fixing one mode of knowing), the subjective character is what mediates between the subject and everything predicated in the science, not by virtual containment or causality but by mediating its reception of attributions. This fits quia and propter quid sciences, sciences of whole and parts, and sciences of partless subjects: truths reduce to the subject immediately ('a syllogism has three terms') or through its parts. Proof: every scientific proposition is per se (first mode, definition of the defined; second, attribute of the subject; fourth, attribute of the subject's definition), and no per se proposition contains an extraneous, non-mediating character ('white man is an animal' is not per se). Since the subject receives per se predication of its principles, parts, species and attributes, and through its first parts of theirs, the subjective character is what mediates all these and is not extraneous to the subject.
claims: The subjective character is what mediates the subject's reception of all the science's predicates.
Mediation here is reception of attribution, not virtual containment or causality.
Every scientific proposition is per se and contains no extraneous character.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3026.summary: Further proof: a character whose removal leaves the science and its propositions intact is not subjective, and one whose removal destroys them is. Removing the character by which the subject has parts and principles removes the whole science, so the mediating character is the subjective one.
claims: The subjective character is the one whose removal destroys the science.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3059.summary: Rubric announcing that deity is the subjective character of theology.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3066.summary: Second proposition: deity is the formal subjective character of theology, since it mediates between God and everything declared and fixes theology's knowable genus and mode. Through deity are attributed to God the three persons (quasi-parts), the essential perfections (understanding, willing), everything under omnipotence (God could create, unite God and man, make a virgin give birth), and every contingent fact under the divine will (the Virgin gave birth, Abraham had two sons). Deity also fixes theology's declarative mode without adherence: if deity could be grasped clearly and properly by natural means the habit would be scientific and adhesive, but since it cannot, theology acquired by natural ability is only declarative. Hence a sixfold division of theology by ways of being divine: by essence, or by participation through assumption (Christ), creation and governance (the world), precept and prohibition (virtues and vices), institution (sacraments), and final fulfillment (beatific vision and love).
claims: Deity is theology's subjective character.
Everything declared in theology, necessary or contingent, is attributed to God through deity.
Theology is declarative because deity cannot be distinctly known by natural means.
Theology divides into six parts by the ways things are divine.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3179.summary: First part of theology: things divine by essence, the unity of God, the Trinity and the like, treated in Sentences book 1.
claims: Book 1 treats things divine by essence.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3188.summary: Second part: things divine by participation through personal assumption, Christ and truths about him, treated at the beginning of book 3.
claims: Book 3 begins with things divine by assumption.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3201.summary: Third part: what is attributed to God under the general relations of creation, governance and conservation, treated in book 2.
claims: Book 2 treats creation, governance and conservation.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3213.summary: Fourth part: what is attributed to God under precept and prohibition (virtues, grace, vices), treated from the middle of book 2 on and from the middle of book 3.
claims: The latter parts of books 2 and 3 treat grace, virtues and vices.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3226.summary: Fifth part: what is attributed to God under institution, the sacraments, treated in book 4.
claims: Book 4 treats the sacraments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3237.summary: Sixth part: the beatific vision, treated in the last treatise of book 4. Scripture cannot be divided by these six considerations, though it orders everything to purely divine things, Christ, the universe, virtues and vices, sacraments, or the final state of beatitude or misery. Its histories and persons serve to authenticate its transmitters or to move people by examples. The six divisions are found in the doctors, each of whom, writing his own theology, treated all six.
claims: The end of book 4 treats the beatific vision.
Scripture is not organized by the six theological considerations, though it relates to them.
Scripture's histories authenticate its authors or offer moral examples.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3289.summary: Rubric announcing that deity as conceived by analogy by the wayfarer is theology's subjective character.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3296.summary: Third proposition: the proper character of deity is what the wayfaring theologian ultimately attributes all truths to. Deity can be understood in three ways.
claims: The wayfarer attributes theological truths to the proper character of deity.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3312.summary: First way: under general concepts, such as infinite being or pure actuality; actuality and purity are general characters that also apply to creatures...
claims: Deity can be conceived under general concepts like infinite being or pure act.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3322.summary: ...but when purity is added to actuality the concept is appropriated to deity, which alone is pure actuality and infinite being.
claims: 'Pure act' is appropriated to God though built from general concepts.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3333.summary: Second way: under the proper character of deity clearly and nakedly, either intuitively and beatifically or quasi-imaginatively and scientifically, as said earlier.
claims: Deity can be conceived clearly, intuitively or quasi-imaginatively.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3344.summary: Third way: the proper character of deity conceived obscurely by proportion and analogy, as Aristotle conceives matter. So the wayfarer has a proper concept of deity that underlies 'first and infinite being', 'pure act', 'three persons' and all truths theology declares of God; it declares them of this concept, not of infinite being (rather, infinite being of it). Objections: no concept can come from creatures unless formally or virtually contained in creaturely concepts, and a confused proper concept of God is neither (formally would make it common, virtually would make it less perfect). A confused concept is a diminished one, and a proper concept of deity, however diminished, would be beatific, since more and less do not change species.
claims: The wayfarer has a proper but obscure, analogical concept of deity.
This analogical concept is the substrate of all predicates theology declares of God.
(Objection) A proper concept of God cannot be derived from creatures.
(Objection) Any proper concept of deity would be beatific.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3414.summary: Third objection: the analogical concept is just 'substrate of three persons, infinity, actuality', built from general concepts (being, substrate), so not proper. Replies: first, the confused proper concept is contained in creaturely concepts not virtually or formally but proportionally; the assimilative intellect can form a concept that relates to infinite substance and three persons as triangle relates to three angles. So the intellect can rise from creatures to what is contained in them formally, virtually or proportionally.
claims: (Objection) An analogical concept of God is made of general concepts.
A proportional concept can be derived from creatures without formal or virtual containment.
The intellect is assimilative and can form proportional concepts.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3474.summary: Second reply: a proportional concept is not a distinguishing concept, which grasps the proper character so as to distinguish it from everything else; so it is not beatific.
claims: A proportional concept of deity is not distinctive and so not beatific.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3492.summary: Third reply: what underlies infinity, simplicity and the like differs from the character 'substrate'. That character is general, but what is conceived as substrate of these divine properties is not common. Treated more fully at distinction 22.
claims: The thing conceived as substrate of divine properties is not common, though 'substrate' is.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3513.summary: Rubric announcing that theology, though very broad, does not extend to every knowable truth.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3522.summary: Fourth proposition: theology is the most universal science, broader than metaphysics, but does not extend to every knowable truth.
claims: Theology is broader than metaphysics but not exhaustive of all knowable truth.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3533.summary: Proves the first part: the most universal science is the one to whose subject all caused things are attributed in many ways, and all are attributed to deity as produced from nothing, conserved, governed, ordered to it as end, and exemplified by it, ways in which they are not attributed to being, metaphysics' subject.
claims: All caused things are attributed to deity in more ways than to being.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3557.summary: Proves the second part: there are many knowable truths about things' own natures, but theology concerns them only as they share in creation, governance and the like. Granted that whoever knows deity clearly would know all quiddities in it as exemplar, this does not follow for a declarative habit that knows deity confusedly and analogically; if it knew deity that way it would be scientific and adhesive, not declarative.
claims: Theology treats things' natures only as related to God.
Only clear knowledge of deity would yield knowledge of all things in their exemplar.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3603.summary: Heading of a fifth article (printed within the fourth article's division): bodily substance is the subject of natural science.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3612.summary: Tests the definition of the subjective character against the common claim that natural philosophy's subject is the mobile body or mobile being. Mobility does not mediate the physicist's truths (circularity belongs to the heavens not through mobility; figure, odor and color come by motion efficiently, not as the subjective character). So either mobility is not in the subjective character or the definition is false. Auriol keeps the definition and rejects the common saying. No science studies the opposite of its subject's formal character, though it studies opposite attributes (health and sickness, even and odd), and the physicist considers rest as well as motion. So mobility and rest are opposite attributes, not the subjective character.
claims: Natural philosophy's subject is not the mobile body as such.
No science studies the opposite of its subject's formal character.
Motion and rest are opposed attributes of natural bodies.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3696.summary: Further argument: if mobility is in the subjective character, either as aptitude (a relation), making the subject an accidental unity of substance and relation, or as actual motion, so that a body at rest would leave physics. Both are absurd.
claims: Neither aptitudinal nor actual mobility can be part of physics' subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3727.summary: Further argument: no artisan considers beyond what the subject's formal character requires, yet the physicist considers the rarity of the heavens, the moon's spot, and the unity or plurality of worlds, which mobility does not require. Even if all were at rest, natural science would remain as demonstrating sensible accidents. Confirmed: physics is distinguished from mathematics by defining through sensible matter (Metaphysics VI), which would remain if nothing moved.
claims: Physics would remain even if nothing moved.
Physics is distinguished by definition through sensible matter.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3775.summary: Further argument: no science demonstrates its formal character of its subject, but the physicist proves mobility of body (every mobile is a body, Physics VI; every body is mobile, De caelo I).
claims: Physics demonstrates mobility of body, so mobility is an attribute.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3793.summary: Further argument: motion is a common sensible (De anima II), and the physicist treats sensible body's sensible accidents as attributes and body as subject (Meteorology IV), so mobility too is an attribute.
claims: Motion, as a common sensible, is an attribute of physical bodies.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3817.summary: Further argument from the structure of natural philosophy: the subject of the whole is what has as per se parts the subjects of its parts. Dividing bodily substance without mobility, first come simple and mixed. The five simple bodies (four elements and the fifth essence) compose the world, the subject of De caelo as world, not as mobile, where its ungenerability, incorruptibility and unity are treated.
claims: The subject of all natural philosophy has as parts the subjects of its books.
De caelo treats the world as world, not as mobile.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3854.summary: Continues. Mixed bodies are imperfect (hail, snow) or perfect (minerals, plants, animals). De generatione treats the mixed in general: common accidents in book I (generation, alteration, growth, contact, action, passion, mixture) and principles (the elements as constituents of mixtures) in book II, while De caelo III and IV treat elements as constituents of the world. Imperfect mixtures are the subject of Meteorology I to III, as hail and snow, not as mobile.
claims: De generatione's subject is the mixed as mixed.
Meteorology I to III treat imperfect mixtures.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3920.summary: Continues. Perfect mixtures are living or non-living (minerals, stones, metals). Meteorology IV treats perfect mixture in common (digestion, putrefaction, fusibility, frangibility); the book on minerals treats non-living perfect mixtures as stones and metals, not as mobile.
claims: Meteorology IV treats perfect mixtures in general.
The book of minerals treats stones and metals as such.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e3955.summary: Continues. Living bodies in common are the subject of De anima (living body as living; soul as form, body as matter), with common accidents in the short treatises on life and death, length of life, youth and age. Plants are the subject of De vegetabilibus, animals of De animalibus and the treatises on sleep and on animal motion. Since the species of bodily substance under their own characters are subjects of the partial books, without mobility, though mobility is an attribute of all natural things, bodily substance without mobility is the subject of all physics.
claims: De anima's subject is the living body as living.
Bodily substance, not mobile body, is the subject of natural philosophy.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4007.summary: Further argument: mobile body is to physics as immobile, abstract magnitude to geometry, and immobility and abstraction are not in geometry's subject (continuous permanent quantity as such). Conclusion: bodily substance has sensible properties and accidents, motion the most common, so it fixes one knowable genus where intellect extends to sensibles. Bodily substantiality is the subjective character, and rest, motion and sensible accidents are attributes. Physics I says motion is presupposed and not to be disputed with deniers not because it is the subjective character but because it is self-evident and a general attribute of all bodily substance, like sensibility. So demonstrations from motion (of prime matter, form's distinction, the first principle, the earth's roundness) count as a posteriori, which they would not if motion were the subjective character.
claims: Bodily substantiality is the subjective character of natural philosophy.
Motion is a self-evident general attribute of bodies, not their subjective character.
Demonstrations from motion in physics are a posteriori.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4085.summary: Rubric announcing that speech (vox) as expressive of concepts is the subject of logic.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4092.summary: Tests the definition against common views of logic's subject: the mode of knowing, second intentions, or the syllogism. On these, not everything in logic would belong to its subject. Against second intentions: they are not logic's adequate subject, since grammar and rhetoric also treat them (modes of signifying are second intentions like the predicables; rhetorical speech is one like the dialectical syllogism).
claims: Second intentions are not logic's adequate subject, since grammar and rhetoric also treat them.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4134.summary: Further: second intentions exist only objectively in the soul, and being-in-the-soul belongs to the first philosopher (Metaphysics VI), so second intentions do not define logic.
claims: Being in the soul belongs to metaphysics.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4151.summary: Nor is the syllogism logic's subject, since it does not cover all of logic: the treatises on the categories and on the proposition are principal parts treating incomplex words and propositions as per se intended. Even if no syllogism were possible, they would still be logical knowledge, and removing a science's subject leaves nothing of it.
claims: The syllogism is not logic's subject, since the Categories and Peri hermeneias would survive without it.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4195.summary: Nor is the mode of knowing logic's subject, since it is the way of demonstrating and taking principles, one part of logic (Posterior Analytics).
claims: The mode of knowing is only the subject of the Posterior Analytics.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4211.summary: Further: logic also teaches the mode of disputing (dialectical, sophistical, probative), of stating, predicating and dividing, the common forms of demonstration, syllogism, proposition and division, so the mode of knowing does not exhaust it.
claims: Logic covers disputation, predication and division as well as demonstration.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4242.summary: Nor is being of reason logic's subject, since it exceeds logic: grammar's modes of signifying, parts of speech and congruity are beings of reason, as are rhetoric's matters.
claims: Being of reason is broader than logic.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4258.summary: Further: being of reason is a mode of being treated in Metaphysics VI. Auriol's answer: logic's subject is speech (vox) as expressive of concepts, which is adequate to logic and whose species are subjects of its parts. Incomplex speech expressing simple concepts belongs to the Categories, complex speech expressing composing and dividing to Peri hermeneias, and discursive speech (syllogism) to the 'new logic'. Logic does not exceed this, nor is it exceeded, since the grammarian treats speech for the modes of conceiving its modes of signifying express ('every noun signifies substance with quality') and the rhetorician treats speech as producing delight and assent.
claims: Logic's subject is speech as expressive of concepts.
Its species (incomplex, complex, discursive) are the subjects of logic's parts.
Grammar and rhetoric treat speech under other aspects.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4321.summary: Further: sciences are named from their subjects (arithmetic from number, grammar from letter, harmonics from sound), and logic from logos, speech. Logic is also counted among the three sciences of speech.
claims: Logic's name indicates speech as its subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4338.summary: Further: what is first subject of truth and falsity is logic's subject, since true and false are its general attributes, as healthy and sick are medicine's. Speech as expressing concepts is subject of truth and falsity, since words signify truly or falsely in relation to concepts. Confirmed: truth and falsity belong to speech as sign, to the concept as signified.
claims: True and false are logic's general attributes.
Speech is true or false as expressing concepts.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4367.summary: Further: Aristotle throughout his logic treats speech expressing concepts, as the Categories begin with equivocal, univocal and denominative names and divide incomplex sayables into ten categories, Peri hermeneias begins with noun, verb and sentence, and Prior Analytics defines the syllogism as speech (oratio). So the definition of the subjective character holds and guides us to find each science's formal subject, multitude in arithmetic, magnitude in geometry, and so on. End of the fifth article.
claims: Aristotle's logical works treat signifying speech throughout.
The definition of the subjective character identifies each science's formal subject.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4413.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the first set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4418.summary: Replies to the arguments for Christ as subject. Everything Moses wrote pertaining to Christ does not make Christ the subject, as everything in metaphysics pertains to Socrates (God as end, quiddity as form, act and potency as accidents) without Socrates being its subject. Moses intends Christ not as man but as man assumed by God. The articles on Christ's humanity concern humanity as assumed, which answers the second and third arguments.
claims: Pertaining to something does not make it a science's subject.
Scripture intends Christ as assumed by God, not as mere man.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4462.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the second set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4467.summary: Replies to the 'believable' argument: theology declares believed things, but the believable is not its subject, just as faith concerns believed things but has God, subject of all the articles, as object. Theology by declaring and faith by adhering concern the same object.
claims: Faith and theology share God as object, one adhering and one declaring.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4490.summary: Replies to the revealability argument: theology treats the histories of the kings and patriarchs rather than Roman history not because they were revealed (they were seen and faithfully recorded like Roman history) but because they relate to God as governing, appointing and preordaining or reproving the kings of Israel. This shows the revealable is not theology's subject.
claims: Sacred histories belong to theology because they relate to God's governance, not because they were revealed.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4519.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the third set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4524.summary: Replies to the 'things and signs' argument: every science concerns things (mathematics, physics) or signs (logic, grammar). Theology concerns divine things and signs, and treats them only in relation to God, so God is the subject.
claims: Every science concerns things or signs; theology concerns divine ones only in relation to God.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4557.summary: Replies to the division argument: theology divides by things and signs only materially; formally it divides by different relations to God, or different ways of being divine.
claims: Theology's formal division is by relations to God.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4575.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the fourth set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4580.summary: Replies to the 'divine being' argument: divine being is not first intended with God following; God is first intended and all divine being because of him, so God is the subject.
claims: God is first intended in theology, and divine being consequently.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4599.summary: Replies to the latitude argument: God is as wide as being not formally or predicatively but virtually and reductively, so theology is not inferior or subalternate to metaphysics but superior, regulating it and quasi-subalternating it. It uses metaphysics and physics to declare believed things but is not measured by them; it measures them, showing false whatever conflicts with it and confirming what agrees (Augustine).
claims: God's latitude equals being's virtually and reductively.
Theology regulates metaphysics and physics, judging their conclusions.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4630.summary: Replies to the four-senses argument: theology does not have four objects in the four senses; in each sense it conjectures something about God, drawing out its meaning for God's sake.
claims: The four senses of Scripture share God as object.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4641.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the fifth set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4646.summary: Replies to the argument that God lacks parts, attributes and principles. God has quasi-parts (the three persons, since some things are true of one person and not another), quasi-attributes (perfection-concepts), and a quasi-principle (the quidditative concept from which the persons and perfections could be demonstrated a priori). Or a subject needs only secondary concepts knowable through a quidditative concept that is a principle of knowing, not of being, as in geometry. Or a declarative habit can concern what has no principles, as with first principles (Metaphysics IV).
claims: The persons, perfections and quidditative concept function as quasi-parts, attributes and principle.
A subject needs only principles of knowing, not of being.
A declarative habit can concern what has no principles.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4690.summary: Replies to the division argument: theology is divided not by divisions of God but of what is attributed to him. Sciences divide by their subject in several ways: by subjective parts (natural philosophy by species of body), by integral parts (grammar by letter and word), by principal attributes (geometry by figure and proportion), or by principal modes of attribution (ethics by end, perfecting habits, and direction of human acts). Scripture divides by none of the first three but by principal attributions to God, such as creating and separating (Genesis), liberating (Exodus), and informing by ceremonies and laws (Leviticus).
claims: Sciences can be divided by subjective parts, integral parts, principal attributes, or modes of attribution.
Scripture's books are divided by principal attributions to God.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4790.summary: Replies to the 'one concept of God' argument: there can be several concepts of God, not intrinsic but connotative, as will appear later; this agrees with Aristotle according to Averroes on Metaphysics XII.
claims: God admits several connotative concepts.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4807.summary: Replies to the metaphysics argument: God is not metaphysics' subject but is considered there as first form and last end of all being (Aristotle; Averroes on VII). Or, even if he were, metaphysics would be a different habit from theology, adhesive rather than declarative.
claims: God is considered in metaphysics as first form and end, not as subject.
Metaphysics and theology differ as adhesive and declarative habits.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4829.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the sixth set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4834.summary: Replies to the finite-infinite argument: a habit need not be proportioned to its object in degree of being, only by conformity, so a finite habit can bear on an infinite object, as a finite act does in the blessed.
claims: A finite habit can have an infinite object.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4858.summary: Replies to the glorifier argument: theology determines truths useful for our restoration and glorification, but deity, to which all truths are attributed, is the subjective character, not glorification.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4880.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the seventh set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4885.summary: Replies to the 'good and end' argument: the character of good and end is either what underlies the relation of finality, which is deity, or the relation itself, which is not the noblest character.
claims: The ground of God's goodness and finality is deity.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4904.summary: Replies to the practical-object argument: a speculative habit's object is not the speculable as speculable but the thing itself, and a practical habit's not the operable as operable. So theology's object is God and the supremely lovable character, deity, not lovability.
claims: A habit's object is the thing itself, not its speculability or operability.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4926.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the eighth set of arguments.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4931.summary: Replies to the 'God as unknown' argument: neither faith nor theology has God as unknown for object; though faith concerns things not apparent, non-apparentness is concomitant, not the objective character.
claims: Non-apparentness accompanies faith's object but is not its formal character.

ol96b1-c16729-d1e4947.summary: Replies to the Dionysian argument: theology unites us to God neither as unknown nor as known but as God simply, and through knowledge, not ignorance. Dionysius' dictum refers to imperfect knowledge of God, not total ignorance.
claims: Theology unites us to God through knowledge, not ignorance.
Dionysian negation expresses imperfect knowledge, not ignorance.
